name: Test Loop: Bavarian Quarter
description: A short 2.8 km shakedown loop from home: Viktoria-Luise-Platz, down Martin-Luther-Straße, round Bayerischer Platz and back past Einstein's old address. Perfect for checking GPS, voice, music and pocket mode before the big ride.
intro: Welcome to the test loop. It's under three kilometres — about fifteen minutes — with five short stories and plenty of turns, so it's a good check that directions, music and pocket mode all work. Off we go.
outro: That's the test loop done — welcome back. If the directions and stories came through clearly, you're ready for the big ride.

pois.name: Viktoria-Luise-Platz
pois.text: This is Viktoria-Luise-Platz, named after the only daughter of Kaiser Wilhelm the Second, and laid out around 1900 as a showpiece garden square. A young Billy Wilder lived at number eleven in the late 1920s, years before Hollywood and Some Like It Hot.

pois.name: The Bavarian Quarter
pois.text: Ahead is the Bavarian Quarter, built between about 1900 and 1914 by developers Salomon and Georg Haberland, with streets named after Bavarian towns and gabled houses meant to feel a little like old Nuremberg. So many Jewish doctors, lawyers and artists lived here that it was nicknamed the Jewish Switzerland.

pois.name: Places of Remembrance
pois.text: Watch the lampposts along here. Since 1993 about eighty small signs have hung around the quarter, each with a picture on one side and, on the other, one of the Nazi-era rules imposed on Jewish residents — such as a 1942 ban on Jews keeping pets. The artwork is called Places of Remembrance.

pois.name: Bayerischer Platz U-Bahn
pois.text: Under this square is Bayerischer Platz station on the U4, Berlin's shortest underground line. Schöneberg was still an independent city when it built the line itself, opening it in 1910 — ten years before Schöneberg became part of Greater Berlin.

pois.name: Haberlandstraße 5
pois.text: Just here on Haberlandstraße, at number five, Albert Einstein lived from 1918 until he left Germany at the end of 1932. The building was destroyed in the war, but a plaque marks the spot where the century's most famous physicist came home every evening.
